data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is critically modulated by the interaction of impervious surfaces and sky view factor, meaning the single best mechanism for cross-city variation is the coupling of daytime heat storage with nighttime radiative trapping, which scales non-linearly with built density.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If an area has high thermal mass but open geometry (e.g., a paved parking lot), radiative cooling is efficient and the UHI is weak.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If an area has dense geometry but pervious, low-thermal-mass surfaces (e.g., a dense forest), there is little heat to trap.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If cloud cover or high wind speed overrides both storage and geometry, the synergistic effect is nullified.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The high thermal mass and low albedo of impervious urban surfaces maximize daytime heat storage. At night, this stored heat is released, but a low sky view factor (due to street canyon geometry) traps the longwave radiation. These mechanisms are synergistic: impervious surfaces provide the heat, and dense geometry prevents its radiative escape. The combined effect scales non-linearly with built density.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
